did_you_know.text: Did you know? Amos calls the wealthy women of Samaria “cows of Bashan”—a sharp expression illustrating their luxurious lives—and accuses them of oppressing the poor and crushing the needy.

Did you know? Amos describes the punishment in terms of captivity and humiliation: the women will be taken away in “hooks,” and their fate will be in “fish baskets.” The precise meaning of these terms is uncertain, but it is clearly a description of harsh exile.

Did you know? The command, “Come to Bethel and transgress,” is ironic: Amos refers to worship at Bethel and Gilgal to show that offering sacrifices does not atone for transgression and moral injustice.

Did you know? The people are seemingly commanded to offer “leavened thanksgiving offerings” and proclaim their freewill offerings, but the context makes clear that this is a criticism of showy worship unaccompanied by repentance and justice.

Did you know? The expression “cleanness of teeth” does not refer to oral hygiene but to hunger: when there is no bread, the teeth remain clean because they have not been used for eating. It is a picture of the scarcity that the Lord brings upon Israel’s cities.
Did you know? Amos describes an uneven drought: the Lord sends rain on one city but not on another, and one field receives rain while a nearby field dries up.
Did you know? The water shortage is so severe that two or three cities go to one city to drink, but even there they cannot satisfy their thirst.
Did you know? The disasters described in the chapter include blight, mildew, and locusts, which destroy the fields, gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees.

Did you know? Amos mentions several disasters together: plague, war in which young men are killed and horses are taken, and a foul stench rising from the camps—and each time he emphasizes: “Yet you did not return to me.”

Did you know? After a series of punishments without repentance comes the warning: “Prepare to meet your God, O Israel.” This is a summons to stand before the Lord for a threatening encounter, not an invitation to a festive event.
